Any ongoing experiments on Vortex? Just curious

We did experiment with it. We know the Vortex team well and are excited for their project.

We ended up comparing the performance of vortex with our current columnar format. We found that there was not much difference and that much lower hanging fruits exist for improving aggregate performance in ParadeDB at the query execution level, so we haven’t adopted it yet
Thanks! Maybe no difference at the compression ratio as well?

tantivy implements a few different compression codecs for the fast field columns, so it does a reasonable job there.

the place where things get a little strange is for string fast fields: tantivy uses a global dictionary per-segment, which means that the actual column is a u64 column, and is highly compressed using one of those codecs. the strings themselves in that dictionary are generically compressed, which isn't ideal... but because of the layout, they are (more) rarely needed.
the performance is very good for the cases we're interested in, but as Phil said, there are a few changes we'd like to make in the medium term which might mean we explore it again.

        #{where_clause_base}
        #{order_clause}
        #{limit_clause}
      SQL

    else

      begin
        last_score, last_barcode = Base64.decode64(page_token).split('_')
        last_score = last_score.to_f
        raise 'Invalid page token format' unless last_score && last_barcode
        Rails.logger.debug("Paging cursor: score=#{last_score}, barcode=#{last_barcode}")
      rescue ArgumentError, TypeError
        raise 'Invalid page token: unable to decode or parse'
      end

      # Query with cursor-based pagination
      sql = <<~SQL.squish
        #{select_clause}
        #{where_clause_base}
        AND (paradedb.score(barcode) <= ? OR (paradedb.score(barcode) <= ? AND barcode <= ?))
        #{order_clause}
        #{limit_clause}
      SQL
      query_params = [category, query, query, query, *params, last_score, last_score, last_barcode, limit]
    end

    # Log the generated SQL and parameters
    Rails.logger.debug("Executing SQL: #{sql}")
    Rails.logger.debug("Parameters: #{query_params.inspect}")

> • If a column is not fast, what performance difference should I expect on large result sets?
in EXPLAIN, you will see a `Normal` scan rather than a `FastField*` scan

the performance difference between the two depends on the width of the row:

if you have a very narrow row, then getting the row from Postgres' heap isn't so bad, because most of each fetch actually pulls in data that you need (not much of the read is wasted on columns you're not using.)

if you have a very wide row, then (modulo TOAST), getting the row from columnar storage can be much more dense, because you're fetching _exactly_ that column contiguously.

it also depends how much your WHERE clause eliminates: if the result is a small fraction of the total, then the per-row density doesn't matter as much, because you'll rarely get the advantage of read-ahead (where fetching one row conveniently also buffers the next one for you)

> 1. HNSW index-based searches can't take advantage of pre-filtering in a meaningful way. Searching for vectors with HNSW always first runs the index search, fetches the results, and only then applies the filter. HNSW will search *all* vectors for your search query, return a limited amount of results, and only then apply your filter on team.
